title: Algebraic fractions
examples: When do I need to find a common denominator?
Can I simplify before I add the fractions together?
What if the denominator is x squared plus one?

explain.say: Today we learn to simplify algebraic fractions. This means making them as simple as possible. We look for common factors in the top and bottom.
To simplify, you must factorise the numerator and the denominator. Then you cancel out any matching factors. For example, six x squared divided by three x squared simplifies to two x.
Adding or subtracting algebraic fractions needs a common denominator. You must find the least common multiple of the denominators. If you have one over x plus two over x, the common denominator is x.
Solving equations with fractions requires clearing the fractions first. You multiply every term by the least common denominator. For example, one over x equals two over x, so x equals 2.

faq.q: Do I always have to factorise everything first?
faq.a: Yes, factorising is the first step for both simplifying and adding. It helps you see the common factors clearly. You might also hear this called 'breaking down the expression'.
asks: Must I factorise the top and bottom?

faq.q: If the denominators are different, what is the common denominator?
faq.a: The common denominator is the least common multiple of all the individual denominators. Think of it like finding the smallest number that both denominators divide into evenly. You might also hear this called 'LCM'.
asks: How do I find the common denominator?

faq.q: When I solve an equation, can I multiply by the denominators?
faq.a: Yes, multiplying every single term by the common denominator clears all the fractions. This turns the equation into one with only whole numbers. Be careful not to multiply any terms by zero.
asks: How do I get rid of the fractions in an equation?
What is the easiest way to solve this equation?

faq.q: Can I cancel out terms that are not in the same position?
faq.a: No, you can only cancel out factors that are exactly the same in both the numerator and the denominator. For example, x over x cancels, but x over x plus one does not.
asks: Is it okay to cancel parts of the fraction?

faq.q: What if a denominator is just a number?
faq.a: If a denominator is just a number, you treat it like a single factor. You can then use standard fraction rules to find the common denominator. For instance, one over two plus one over three needs a common denominator of six.
asks: What if I have a number in the bottom?
How do I handle constant denominators?

facts: To add fractions, you must have a common denominator.
Simplifying means dividing out common factors from top and bottom.
When solving equations, multiplying by the LCD clears the fractions.
You can only cancel factors that appear in both the numerator and the denominator.

quiz.say: Simplify this fraction: (x squared plus two) over (x squared plus two).
quiz.why: The numerator and the denominator are identical factors, so they cancel out leaving just one.

wrong.1: This is wrong because you cannot cancel out entire binomials unless they are the only terms.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the fraction equals one for all values where the denominator is not zero.
wrong.3: This is wrong because you must cancel the whole factor, not just one part of it.

quiz.say: What is the result of adding one over x plus three over x?
quiz.why: Since the denominators are the same, you simply add the numerators together.

wrong.0: This is wrong because you cannot add the denominators together.
wrong.1: This is wrong because you have not performed the required addition.
wrong.3: This is wrong because you forgot to add the numerators together.

quiz.say: Solve for x: 2 over (x plus 1) equals 6 over (x plus 1).
quiz.why: Subtracting the left side from the right side gives zero equals zero. This means any value of x except -1 is a solution.

wrong.1: This is wrong because substituting 1 gives 2/2 = 6/2, which is not true.
wrong.2: This is wrong because substituting -1 makes the denominators zero, which is not allowed.
wrong.3: This is wrong because the equation simplifies to 2/(0+1) = 6/(0+1), which is 2 = 6, a false statement.
